text:
UC Berkeley official says cooperation, consensus and shared governance hold key to strengthening regional universities Collaboration, rather than competition, backed by strong leadership and shared governance, has been key to building a University of California (UC) system in which all 10 campuses thrive by developing their own strengths.
Darren Cooke, chief innovation and entrepreneurship officer at UC Berkeley, emphasized the importance of strong leadership and a shared governing structure in bringing universities together while allowing each to build on its own strengths.
"Every one is amazing, right, and has its own strengths, and I think that's the key. Every one has its own strengths," Cooke said during an interview with The Korea Times.
The UC system offers lessons for Korea as the government seeks to strengthen regional flagship national universities and develop them into institutions capable of competing with Seoul National University.
The UC system brings together 10 campuses, including Berkeley, UCLA and UC San Diego, under a single governing structure while allowing each to develop its own academic and research strengths.
"Most systems have one flagship, like one best campus of all of them," Cooke said, noting that UC, by contrast, has 10 flagships.
He attributed the system's collaborative approach partly to its unified governance, with the Board of Regents overseeing all 10 campuses and the UC Office of the President coordinating efforts across the network.
Cooke acknowledged that establishing a unified governing structure could be challenging, emphasizing that building consensus and a willingness to cooperate among universities would be crucial.
"My guess is you'd have to get consensus and get different groups to want to work together rather than have unified governance," he said.
He also credited the UC system's leadership with fostering a culture of collaboration, in which campuses view one another as partners rather than competitors.
As chair of the UC President's Entrepreneurship Network Council, Cooke is now seeking to expand collaboration across the entire UC system.
The council oversees systemwide programs, including funding to help researchers turn their discoveries into commercial opportunities, support for international startup founders and awards recognizing innovation.
More recently, Cooke introduced a new initiative, bringing together innovation leaders from all 10 campuses to share successful programs, exchange expertise and identify areas where they can support one another.
The initiative has already opened opportunities for cooperation between campuses, including UC Santa Barbara and UC Merced, that might otherwise have gone unexplored.
“Unless you convened a group like that, they wouldn’t have the opportunity to even discuss it,” he said.
Cooke said the goal is to replicate Berkeley's collaborative approach across the broader UC system, allowing campuses to learn from one another and make better use of their collective strengths.
He said stronger university-led startup ecosystems could help regional universities attract talent and investment, but retaining entrepreneurs would also require support from local governments.
He pointed to UC Berkeley's efforts to work with city officials to create a more "founder-friendly" environment, including better infrastructure and policies that encourage startups to stay and grow locally.
"I think that could be translated to Korea," he said, urging local governments to take a more proactive approach to supporting entrepreneurs.
